The flaw is in libcurl's wolfSSL, wolfSSH or OpenSSL 3 provider code. The image's libcurl (libcurl3t64-gnutls, used by git) is built against GnuTLS and libssh2, so that code is not in it.

The flaw is in libcurl's FTP, TFTP, IMAP/POP3/SMTP, LDAP, SCP/SFTP or WebSocket code. libcurl's only user in the image is git, and the sidecar restricts git to http, https, git and ssh (GIT_ALLOW_PROTOCOL in scanner/app/scanners.py), so libcurl only ever runs HTTP(S) transfers.

statements.impact_statement: The flaw leaks or mixes up credentials that libcurl holds (Basic, Digest or Negotiate auth, .netrc, credentials in the URL) between transfers of one process. git in the sidecar holds none: scan targets with credentials in the URL are rejected (scanner/app/target_validation.py), there is no .netrc, no Kerberos ticket and no credential prompt (GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0), and a SCANNER_AUTH token travels as an http.extraHeader, which libcurl sends as a plain header. Each clone runs in its own git process.

Both flaws need an HTTP proxy: one leaks libcurl-held origin credentials to the proxy, the other keeps cleared proxy credentials. Hecate configures no proxy, and git hands libcurl no origin credentials (a SCANNER_AUTH token is an http.extraHeader, which libcurl does not send in the CONNECT request). GO-2026-5932 is not a single flaw: it marks the whole golang.org/x/crypto/openpgp package as unmaintained and unsafe by design. govulncheck finds the package in this upstream binary; which of its code paths use it (most likely go-git's commit-signature support) is not established yet. It goes away when the upstream project moves to a maintained OpenPGP library.
